transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. How can I help you today?

Hi Dr. Smith. I'm here because I just can’t sit through long production meetings or edit sessions anymore—I keep getting up and pacing even when I know I should stay in my seat. It's starting to cause some issues with my colleagues, and I really need to figure out why I can't seem to stay put.
Have you felt restless or on edge for most of the day, nearly every day, or do these urges mainly happen during stressful situations like meetings?

It actually happens outside of work too, not just during those stressful meetings. Even on my days off, I feel this crawling, pent-up energy and can't sit on the couch to relax for more than ten minutes before I'm up cleaning or reorganizing. It feels like I'm constantly on the go, no matter where I am.
Have you felt this way since you were a child, or is this something that started more recently in adulthood?

It actually goes all the way back to childhood; even in elementary school, teachers told my parents I couldn’t stay in my seat and kept getting up to sharpen pencils or wander around. It's always been a part of me, but it has only become a major issue recently because my new job responsibilities require me to sit through so many long meetings.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F90.0", "F41.1"], but based on this conversation, F41.1 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder) seems less likely because the patient's restlessness is not limited to stressful situations and has been present since childhood, which is more consistent with a neurodevelopmental disorder. The lifelong course, onset in childhood, and pervasive nature of motor restlessness and inability to remain seated strongly support a diagnosis of F90.0 (Hyperkinetic disorder). Therefore, the current candidate list is narrowed to F90.0.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a lifelong pattern of motor restlessness and inability to remain seated, present in both childhood and adulthood, across multiple settings, with onset before age 12 and causing functional impairment in occupational contexts. This is consistent with the core symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation.
